The first part of losing weight and getting fit is assessing where you are at, what your goals are and how you intend to get there. This is not too critical, but it needs to be done. Your goals, fitness level, circumstances, everything will change over time. But you must have an idea of where you want to go if you ever intend to move towards your goals. So here we go.

Assessment

  1. Check your weight and height and see where you're at. In the morning, after you pee, strip naked (or in your underwear if you're shy in your own bathroom) and weigh yourself. You should also check your height, no cheating. Take these numbers and compare yourself to a height/weight chart like this one. These numbers are accurate for about 95-99% of you. Unless you're mainlining creatine and eating whole chickens while you bench press small cars your muscle mass is not going to make that big a difference to skew the numbers by much. If you come up as morbidly obese accept that this is where you are. Have yourself a little cry or do a little prayer and accept where you're at. Accepting your weight and moving on every day is the hardest part of your diet and exercise. If your head is not in the game YOU are not in the game...and you will gain weight and become morbidly obese again. I know this is a pretty crappy situation, but its not going to change by looking the other way. Take control of your life, don't let your life control you.

  2. Take pictures. You don't have to show anyone. Once you hit your goals you'll definitely want to though. But that's for later. Starting off you want to take underwear pictures. User the exact same location with the exact same camera with the exact same lighting in the exact same underwear (be sure to wash them). You will want to take at least six pictures:

    • Front unflexed and flexed
    • Side unflexed and flexed
    • Back unflexed and flexed
      If you want to take pics of other specific focus areas go ahead, but remember that you CAN NOT spot reduce fat. Fat is what fat does. You can build up the muscle underneath fat, but it will stay where it chooses. Now, don't take any more pictures for a month. Do these six pictures every month, for like, ever. They won't always be kind and sometimes the next month may look worse, but this is all part of owning your own body. Don't be overly critical of the pictures, but know what they look like and understand what you need to do to make them look better.

  3. Measurements - One thing that can help you mentally if you're hypercritical of your pictures is measuring yourself. Go buy a tape measure and measure your neck, chest, your waist and any other body part that you'd like to look at. If you measure yourself the same way every time you're going to see a mathematical reduction if you're losing weight. It's gonna happen unless you're measuring wrong. Speaking of which, watch these:

    • Basic Women Measurements
    • Basic Men Measurements
      An alternate method of measuring BMI is by tape measurements. This can be found here.

NOTE: If there are major issues with something posted here let me know so I can correct it. I'm far from perfect and can always use a second pair of eyes.

Diet

Here's a little secret: You are ALWAYS on a diet, you're just not tracking it. You can't stop. It may be a good or bad diet, you're always doing it. You're always either eating or not. Get over the stigma of the word. A single word should not hang you up and freak you out. You never start a diet because you never stopped. You modify your diet.

  1. To do that you'll need a little more assessment in the way of something called your Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE). There are many sites out there that will try and give you a general idea of what your TDEE or Basic Metabolic Rate are. Some people have good luck with these, but they always give me astronomical numbers that would make me exceptionally obese. One calculator I've found that is fairly accurate to what will work is setting up your My Fitness Pal profile. Use the calorie capabilities involved with this, but be ready to tweak the macronutrients. It's a starting point, but in reality can mean very little. Your body is the absolute value in this equation. This will take time and readjustment. If you are losing weight and don't want to gnaw off the arm of a baby then keep your calories the same. If you're gaining weight then you need to reduce your calories. I'll explain how to do this.

  2. Measure everything. If you think you guessed right about how much you're eating you're WRONG! Everybody messes this up. The mist highly trained nutritionists mess this up. Unless your hand comes with tattooed measurement graduations and your elbow has been replaced with a scale you're not accurate. You can't eyeball this. Measure and/or weigh everything, preferably weigh it. There are a couple tricks you can use though. If you're into preparation (next number) you can measure your containers. If you're on the go you can just grab a container and have a general idea of how much food it is. You already know that Container Y is X cups. The other trick is with determining graduations. A cup is not a heaping cup. It is level. The same goes for a tea/tablespoon. If it's rounded you're miscalculating. This can straight up put you over calories every single day. Measuring accurately is quite possibly the single most frustrating piece of the weight loss puzzle. If you're stuck and you think you're eating the right amount of food and you're not losing, this is number one, hands down, the first place to look.

  3. Preparation and planning will take you much further than simply winging it. Most people who succeed in their fitness goals have a structured preparation plan that plots their meals for a week. In general you can mix and match, but you can easily spare a few hours on a Sunday or whenever to cook up a couple family sized meals you stick in containers for when you're supposed to eat. This is the perfect time to measure and calculate your food. Some people go as far as sticking labels on the containers with nutritional info on them. A few hours of mass prep over the weekend can mean zero prep during the week. Seriously, if you plan it out right you'll have none to do. Saving you so much time to surf voat, or reddit, or...wait for it...working out.

  4. Macronutrients can do some pretty stellar things if you use them appropriately. For those that are unfamiliar, your macronutrients are carbohydrates, fat and protein and depending on who you ask, fiber. Please read this short and concise article about macronutrients from The McKinley Health Center. Did you eat up all your calories for the day but still starving? I bet you at them all in bagels and honey buns, didn't you? Carbs aren't that great for satiety. You know what kicks butt in this department? Protein and fiber fill you up for the long haul. If you have the time, read up on the Fullness Factor. Now if you followed the My Fitness Pal link earlier and made an account you probably went with the default macronutrient ratio. You're going to want to pretty much double the automatic protein percentage they give you. Pull it all from your carbohydrate percentage. If you're fat you already have a surplus and can stand to cut some out some carbs.Why? Because the next section is all about working out and becoming a gym rat. You're going to love the gym. It may seem like a big, dangerous, scary place with a bunch of haters, but you're wrong...and you're going to need a lot of protein and fat to feed them muscles you're growing. Anyway, this is the macronutrient ratios I'm using. Tweak yours as appropriate:

    • Carbohydrates (135g) - 30%
    • Fats (70g) - 35%
    • Protein ( 158g) - 35%

  5. Divergent diets are not frowned upon. They do, however, require a bunch of research and knowledge that surpasses just knowing what a macronutrient is. They DO work, when followed appropriately. I have seen people have great success with keto, paleo, 5/2 fasting, etc. However, you need to do your research before you jump into them or you will fail. There are subverses and subreddits alike that will help you with whatever diet you're planning on jumping on board with. Just remember that this is something you'll need to live with. They're not halfhearted endeavors. You can't just pop into ketosis on a whim and start shedding pounds. You need to know how you're going to go about them before you start. Again, preparation is key.

  6. Starvation mode is a fallacy. Well, in the common understanding it's a fallacy. I'd like to rework the term for my own purposes, but let me first explain why it's false. Starvation mode is when your body has used all of its glucose reserves and starts eating other sources. This takes like 4-5 days of eating 500 or less calories per day to kick in. You're not doing that. What you are doing is shorting yourself a few hundred calories under your daily budget, eating six ho-ho's and "forgetting" to track them, because you were hungry and embarrassed. Try and eat at or close to the calories you've scheduled unless you know for a fact you're not going to enter "starvation mode" later and start binging.

  7. OOPS! you did it again. You ate a bagel and went over. Yeah, okay, it's not the end of the world. So you went over your calories by a couple hundred. No worries. Don't freak out. Don't give up a whole diet change because you caved and had a twinkie. One twinkie does not a box of twinkies make. It's perfectly acceptable to cheat. Everybody cheats. They just don't cheat in large amounts. Have a few chips, just don't eat the whole bag. Letting yourself go is uncontrolled binging and not cool. Getting the right macronutrients will help you, but you're still going to mess up from time to time. Realize this and adjust accordingly.

This is actually pretty much exactly what's happening here. I think we agree but you may be misinterpreting my argument or I'm not making myself clear enough. Just to phrase this in the same context:

TWC has the raw goods, and is like the farm. TWC sells access to it's consumers through direct connections with it's network. A transit provider (in this case, a lettuce distributor), buys a large direct connection to TWC for a lower price per Mbps, as well as connections to a variety of other ISPs (similar to how a distributor would buy a large amount of lettuce for a lower price per head than someone who is only buying 5 heads, although in this case the ISP may give the connection for free in exchange for the ability to connect to the other ISPs that link with the transit provider). Then a local ISP (similar to a grocery store) buys access to the transit provider's network (like buying lettuce from a distributor), which allows them to interconnect with other ISPs. CNS is then expected to buy bandwidth (lettuce) from that ISP.

CNS also has the option to buy directly from the transit provider (distributor) or directly from the ISP they want access to (the farmer), but with the exception that it will likely be more expensive because instead of buying a portion of a much larger batch that were purchased for a low price, they are now buying small amounts directly. On the up side for them, they get a better connection (the lettuce doesn't sit in a distributor's warehouse and wilt).

What CNS is doing in this scenario is coming and saying "You're giving the distributor a way better deal than you're giving me, and even though I'm not buying in bulk, I expect you to give me the same price." In Internet terms, the transit providers and other ISPs are giving service (i.e. I won't charge you for connecting to my network if you don't charge me for connecting to yours) in lieu of payment. CNS is offering more or less nothing in exchange for their connection, which I think is problematic.

The one exception to this is utterly massive service providers like Google (who isn't necessarily connected because they're an ISP) or Netflix. They get distributor rates primarily because of how large a service they are. That, you could certainly say is unfair. The thing is, no one particularly gives a shit if CNS is slow, in the sense that it will be seen as a failing of CNS. If Google and Netflix are slow, people will notice and blame the ISP. It's mutually beneficial for both Google/Netflix and the ISP. With CNS, such an agreement is only beneficial to CNS. This is the gray area to me. ISPs should be able to peer without paying, but endpoints are being treated differently.

This is actually pretty much exactly what's happening here. I think we agree but you may be misinterpreting my argument or I'm not making myself clear enough. Just to phrase this in the same context:

TWC has the raw goods, and is like the farm. TWC sells access to it's consumers through direct connections with it's network. A transit provider (in this case, a lettuce distributor), buys a large direct connection to TWC for a lower price per Mbps, as well as connections to a variety of other ISPs (similar to how a distributor would buy a large amount of lettuce for a lower price per head than someone who is only buying 5 heads, although in this case the ISP may give the connection for free in exchange for the ability to connect to the other ISPs that link with the transit provider). Then a local ISP (similar to a grocery store) buys access to the transit provider's network (like buying lettuce from a distributor), which allows them to interconnect with other ISPs. CNS is then expected to buy bandwidth (lettuce) from that ISP.

CNS also has the option to buy directly from the transit provider (distributor) or directly from the ISP they want access to (the farmer), but with the exception that it will likely be more expensive because instead of buying a portion of a much larger batch that were purchased for a low price, they are now buying small amounts directly. On the up side for them, they get a better connection (the lettuce doesn't sit in a distributor's warehouse and wilt).

What CNS is doing in this scenario is coming and saying "You're giving the distributor a way better deal than you're giving me, and even though I'm not buying in bulk, I expect you to give me the same price." In Internet terms, the transit providers and other ISPs are giving service (i.e. I won't charge you for connecting to my network if you don't charge me for connecting to yours) in lieu of payment. CNS is offering more or less nothing in exchange for their connection, which I think is problematic.

The one exception to this is utterly massive service providers like Google (who isn't necessarily connected because they're an ISP) or Netflix. They get distributor rates primarily because of how large a service they are. That, you could certainly say is unfair. The thing is, no one particularly gives a shit if CNS is slow, in the sense that it will be seen as a failing of CNS. If Google and Netflix are slow, people will notice and blame the ISP. It's mutually beneficial for both Google/Netflix and the ISP. With CNS, such an agreement is only beneficial to CNS. This is the gray area to me. ISPs should be able to peer without paying, but endpoints are being treated differently.
